chapters.title: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
paragraphs: A fortnight later, by excellent good fortune, the doctor gave one of his pleasant dinners to some five or six old friends, all intelligent, reputable men and all judges of good wine; and Mr. Utterson so arranged things that he stayed behind after the others had left. This was nothing new—it had happened dozens of times before. Where Utterson was liked, he was liked well. Hosts loved to keep the dry lawyer a while longer, once the light-hearted and loose-tongued had already had their foot on the threshold; they liked to sit a bit in his unobtrusive company, practicing for solitude, sobering their minds in the man's rich silence after the expense and strain of gaiety. Dr. Jekyll was no exception to this rule; and as he now sat on the opposite side of the fire—a large, well-built, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something faintly sly about him perhaps, but every mark of ability and kindness—you could see by his expression that he felt a sincere and warm affection for Mr. Utterson.
“I’ve been wanting to speak to you, Jekyll,” Utterson began. “You know that will of yours?”

A close observer might have noticed that the subject was unwelcome; but the doctor carried it off lightly. “My poor Utterson,” he said, “you’re unlucky to have a client like me. I never saw a man so troubled as you were by my will—except perhaps that rigid pedant Lanyon, over what he called my scientific heresies. Oh, I know he’s a good fellow—you needn’t frown—an excellent fellow, and I always mean to see more of him; but a rigid pedant all the same; an ignorant, loud-mouthed pedant. I’ve never been more disappointed in any man than in Lanyon.”
“You know I never approved of it,” Utterson went on, refusing to be drawn onto the new subject.
“My will? Yes, of course I know that,” said the doctor, a little sharply. “You’ve told me so.”
“Well, I’m telling you again,” the lawyer continued. “I’ve been learning something about young Hyde.”
The large, handsome face of Dr. Jekyll went pale to the very lips, and a darkness came over his eyes. “I don’t care to hear any more,” he said. “This is a subject I thought we’d agreed to drop.”
“What I heard was appalling,” said Utterson.

“It can’t change anything. You don’t understand my position,” the doctor replied, with a certain unevenness in his manner. “I’m painfully placed, Utterson; my position is a very strange one—a very strange one indeed. It’s one of those situations that talking can’t mend.”
“Jekyll,” said Utterson, “you know me: I’m a man who can be trusted. Tell me the whole of it in confidence, and I have no doubt I can get you out of it.”

“My good Utterson,” said the doctor, “this is very good of you—downright good of you—and I can’t find words to thank you for it. I believe you completely; I’d trust you before any man alive, yes, before myself, if I could make the choice; but truly, it isn’t what you imagine; it isn’t as bad as that; and just to set your good heart at rest, I’ll tell you one thing: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde. I give you my word on that; and I thank you again and again; and I’ll just add one more word, Utterson, that I’m sure you’ll take the right way: this is a private matter, and I beg you to let it rest.”
Utterson thought a little, looking into the fire.
“I’ve no doubt you’re perfectly right,” he said at last, rising to his feet.

“Well, but since we’ve touched on this business—and for the last time, I hope,” the doctor went on, “there’s one point I’d like you to understand. I really do take a great interest in poor Hyde. I know you’ve seen him; he told me so; and I’m afraid he was rude. But I do sincerely take a great, a very great interest in that young man; and if I’m taken away, Utterson, I want you to promise me that you’ll put up with him and see that he gets what’s due to him. I think you would, if you knew everything; and it would be a weight off my mind if you’d promise.”
“I can’t pretend I’ll ever like him,” said the lawyer.
“I’m not asking that,” Jekyll pleaded, laying his hand on the other’s arm. “I’m only asking for justice; I’m only asking you to help him for my sake, when I’m no longer here.”
Utterson let out an unwilling sigh. “Well,” he said, “I promise.”

chapters.title: The Carew Murder Case
paragraphs: Nearly a year later, in the month of October, 18—, London was shaken by a crime of such singular ferocity, and made all the more notorious by the high standing of the victim, that the details were few but startling. A maidservant living alone in a house not far from the river had gone up to bed around eleven. Though fog rolled over the city in the small hours, the early part of the night was cloudless, and the lane her window looked onto was lit brilliantly by the full moon. It seems she had a romantic streak, for she sat down on her trunk, which stood right under the window, and fell into a daydream. Never, she used to say afterward, with tears streaming down her face as she told the story—never had she felt more at peace with everyone or thought more kindly of the world. And as she sat there, she noticed an aged, handsome, white-haired gentleman drawing near along the lane, and another gentleman, a very small one, advancing to meet him, to whom at first she paid little attention. When they came within speaking distance—right beneath the maid’s window—the older man bowed and greeted the other with a very charming show of politeness. It didn’t seem as if what he was saying was especially important; in fact, from the way he pointed, it sometimes looked as though he were only asking directions; but the moon shone on his face as he spoke, and the girl was pleased to watch it, for it seemed to breathe such an innocent, old-fashioned kindness of nature—yet with something lofty in it too, the self-possession of a man well satisfied with himself. Presently her eye wandered to the other man, and she was surprised to recognize a certain Mr. Hyde, who had once visited her master and for whom she had taken a dislike. He had a heavy cane in his hand, which he was playing with idly; but he answered not a word, and seemed to listen with badly hidden impatience. And then all at once he broke into a great blaze of anger, stamping his foot, brandishing the cane, and carrying on—as the maid described it—like a madman. The old gentleman stepped back, looking very surprised and a little hurt; and at that Mr. Hyde flew past all restraint and clubbed him to the ground. And the next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and raining down a storm of blows, under which the bones could be heard breaking and the body jumped on the roadway. At the horror of these sights and sounds, the maid fainted.

It was two o’clock when she came to herself and called the police. The murderer was long gone by then; but his victim lay in the middle of the lane, mangled almost beyond belief. The stick with which the crime had been done, though it was made of some rare, tough, heavy wood, had snapped in two under the force of this senseless cruelty; and one splintered half had rolled into the gutter nearby—the other, no doubt, had been carried off by the murderer. A purse and a gold watch were found on the victim, but no cards or papers except a sealed and stamped envelope, which he had probably been carrying to the post, and which bore the name and address of Mr. Utterson.

This was brought to the lawyer the next morning before he was even out of bed; and no sooner had he seen it and been told the circumstances than he set his lips grimly. “I’ll say nothing until I’ve seen the body,” he said. “This may be very serious. Be good enough to wait while I dress.” And with the same grave face he hurried through breakfast and drove to the police station where the body had been taken. As soon as he entered the cell, he nodded.
“Yes,” he said, “I recognize him. I’m sorry to say this is Sir Danvers Carew.”

“Good God, sir,” exclaimed the officer, “is it possible?” And the next moment his eyes lit up with professional ambition. “This will make a great deal of noise,” he said. “And perhaps you can help us find the man.” And he briefly described what the maid had seen, and showed him the broken stick.

Mr. Utterson had already flinched at the name of Hyde; but when the stick was laid before him, he could doubt no longer—broken and battered as it was, he recognized it as one he had himself given, many years before, to Henry Jekyll.
“Is this Mr. Hyde a small man?” he asked.
“Particularly small and particularly wicked-looking, is what the maid calls him,” said the officer.
Mr. Utterson thought for a moment; then, raising his head, “If you’ll come with me in my cab,” he said, “I think I can take you to his house.”

It was by this time about nine in the morning, and the first fog of the season. A great chocolate-colored pall hung low over the sky, but the wind kept charging and scattering these massed vapors, so that as the cab crawled from street to street, Mr. Utterson witnessed a remarkable range of shades and degrees of twilight; for here it would be dark as the end of evening, and there a glow of rich, lurid brown, like the light of some strange fire; and here, for a moment, the fog would break apart entirely and a ragged shaft of daylight would slip in between the swirling clouds. The dismal district of Soho, glimpsed through these shifting gaps, with its muddy streets, its shabby foot traffic, and its lamps, which had never been put out or had been relit to fight off this mournful return of darkness, seemed to the lawyer's eyes like a district of some city in a nightmare. His thoughts, besides, were of the gloomiest sort; and when he glanced at his companion in the cab, he felt something of that dread of the law and its officers which can, at times, seize even the most honest of men.

As the cab pulled up at the address given, the fog lifted a little and showed him a dingy street, a gin shop, a cheap French eating house, a shop selling penny novels and twopenny salads, many ragged children huddled in doorways, and many women of many nationalities going out, key in hand, for a morning glass of drink; and the next moment the fog settled back down over that part of town, brown as umber, and cut him off from his disreputable surroundings. This was the home of Henry Jekyll's favorite—a man who stood to inherit a quarter of a million pounds.

An ivory-faced, silver-haired old woman opened the door. She had a wicked face, smoothed over by hypocrisy, but her manners were excellent. Yes, she said, this was Mr. Hyde's house, but he wasn't in; he had come home very late that night, but had gone out again within the hour; there was nothing unusual in that, his habits were very irregular, and he was often away—for instance, it had been nearly two months since she'd seen him until yesterday.

“Very well, then, we want to see his rooms,” said the lawyer; and when the woman began protesting it was impossible, “I'd better tell you who this person is,” he added. “This is Inspector Newcomen of Scotland Yard.”
A flash of ugly delight crossed the woman's face. “Ah!” she said, “he's in trouble! What's he done?”
Mr. Utterson and the inspector exchanged glances. “He doesn't seem a very popular man,” the inspector observed. “Now then, my good woman, just let this gentleman and me have a look around.”

In the whole extent of the house, which apart from the old woman stood otherwise empty, Mr. Hyde had used only a couple of rooms; but these were furnished with luxury and good taste. A closet was stocked with wine; the silverware was fine, the linen elegant; a good painting hung on the wall, a gift, Utterson supposed, from Henry Jekyll, who was quite the connoisseur; and the carpets were thick-piled and pleasing in color. At that moment, however, the rooms showed every sign of having been recently and hastily ransacked; clothes lay scattered on the floor with their pockets turned inside out; locked drawers stood open; and on the hearth lay a heap of gray ash, as though a great many papers had been burned. From these embers the inspector dug out the unburned stub of a green checkbook, which had survived the fire; the other half of the stick was found behind the door; and since this confirmed his suspicions, the officer declared himself delighted. A visit to the bank, where several thousand pounds were found lying to the murderer's credit, completed his satisfaction.

“You may depend on it, sir,” he told Mr. Utterson: “I have him in my hand. He must have lost his head, or he'd never have left the stick, and above all never have burned the checkbook. Why, money's life itself to a man like that. We've nothing to do but wait for him at the bank and put out the handbills.”

This last, however, wasn't so easy to manage; for Mr. Hyde had had few close acquaintances—even the maid's employer had seen him only twice; his family could nowhere be traced; he had never been photographed; and the few who could describe him disagreed widely, as ordinary witnesses will. On only one point were they in agreement: the haunting sense of some indescribable deformity that the fugitive left with everyone who saw him.

chapters.title: Incident of the Letter
paragraphs: It was late in the afternoon when Mr. Utterson made his way to Dr. Jekyll's door, where Poole let him in at once and led him down through the kitchen quarters and across a yard that had once been a garden, to the building known indifferently as the laboratory or the dissecting rooms. The doctor had bought the house from the heirs of a celebrated surgeon, and since his own interests ran more to chemistry than to anatomy, he had changed the use of the block at the bottom of the garden. This was the first time the lawyer had been received in that part of his friend's quarters, and he eyed the dingy, windowless building with curiosity, looking around with an uneasy sense of strangeness as he crossed the operating theater—once crowded with eager students and now standing gaunt and silent, its tables loaded with chemical apparatus, its floor littered with crates and packing straw, the light falling dimly through the grimy skylight. At the far end, a flight of stairs led up to a door covered in red baize; and through this Mr. Utterson was finally shown into the doctor's private study. It was a large room lined with glass cabinets, furnished among other things with a full-length mirror and a desk, and looking out over the courtyard through three dusty, iron-barred windows. A fire burned in the grate; a lamp stood lit on the mantel, for even indoors the fog had begun to settle thick; and there, close by the warmth, sat Dr. Jekyll, looking deathly ill. He did not rise to greet his visitor, but held out a cold hand and welcomed him in a changed voice.
“And now,” said Mr. Utterson, as soon as Poole had left them, “you've heard the news?”
The doctor shuddered. “They were shouting it in the square,” he said. “I heard them from my dining room.”
“One word,” said the lawyer. “Carew was my client, but so are you, and I want to know what I'm doing. You haven't been mad enough to hide this fellow?”

“Utterson, I swear to God,” cried the doctor, “I swear to God I will never set eyes on him again. I give you my word of honor that I'm done with him in this world. It's all over. And in truth he doesn't need my help; you don't know him as I do; he's safe, he's quite safe; mark my words, he'll never be heard of again.”

The lawyer listened grimly; he didn't like his friend's feverish manner. “You seem quite sure of him,” he said. “And for your sake, I hope you're right. If it came to a trial, your name might come up.”

“I'm quite sure of him,” Jekyll replied. “I have grounds for certainty that I can't share with anyone. But there's one thing you can advise me on. I have—I've received a letter, and I can't decide whether I should show it to the police. I'd like to leave it in your hands, Utterson; you'd judge wisely, I'm sure; I have such great trust in you.”
“You're afraid, I suppose, that it might lead to his capture?” asked the lawyer.
“No,” said the other. “I can't say I care what becomes of Hyde; I'm quite done with him. I was thinking of my own reputation, which this hateful business has rather exposed.”
Utterson mulled this over for a while; he was surprised by his friend's selfishness, and yet relieved by it. “Well,” he said at last, “let me see the letter.”

The letter was written in an odd, upright hand and signed “Edward Hyde”; and it stated, briefly enough, that the writer's benefactor, Dr. Jekyll, whom he had for so long so unworthily repaid for a thousand kindnesses, need feel no alarm for his safety, since he had a means of escape on which he placed complete confidence. The lawyer liked this letter well enough; it cast a better light on the friendship than he had expected, and he blamed himself for some of his past suspicions.
“Have you got the envelope?” he asked.
“I burned it,” Jekyll replied, “before I thought about what I was doing. But it bore no postmark. The note was delivered by hand.”
“Shall I keep this and sleep on it?” asked Utterson.
“I want you to judge for me entirely,” was the reply. “I've lost confidence in myself.”
“Well, I'll think it over,” the lawyer answered. “And now one more thing: was it Hyde who dictated the terms in your will about that disappearance?”
The doctor seemed seized by a fit of faintness; he shut his mouth tight and nodded.
“I knew it,” said Utterson. “He meant to murder you. You had a narrow escape.”
“I've had something far more to the point,” the doctor answered gravely: “I've had a lesson—oh God, Utterson, what a lesson I've had!” And he covered his face for a moment with his hands.

On his way out, the lawyer stopped and had a word or two with Poole. “By the way,” he said, “there was a letter delivered today: what did the messenger look like?” But Poole was certain that nothing had come except by post, “and only circulars at that,” he added.

This news sent the visitor off with his fears renewed. Clearly the letter had come by way of the laboratory door; quite possibly, in fact, it had been written in the study; and if that were so, it had to be judged differently, and handled with more caution. The newsboys, as he walked, were shouting themselves hoarse along the footpaths: “Special edition. Shocking murder of an M.P.” That was the funeral oration for one friend and client; and he couldn't help feeling a certain dread that the good name of another might be dragged down into the whirlpool of the scandal. It was, at the very least, a delicate decision he had to make; and self-reliant as he was by habit, he began to wish for some advice. It wasn't to be had directly; but perhaps, he thought, it might be fished for.

Presently he sat on one side of his own hearth, with Mr. Guest, his head clerk, on the other, and midway between them, at a carefully judged distance from the fire, a bottle of a particular old wine that had lain long unexposed to the sun in the depths of his cellar. The fog still lay sleeping on the wing above the drowned city, where the lamps glimmered like gems; and through the smother of these fallen clouds, the procession of the town's life still rolled on through its great arteries with a sound like a mighty wind. But the room was cheerful with firelight. In the bottle the acids had long since mellowed; the deep color had softened with age, the way the hue grows richer in stained glass windows; and the glow of hot autumn afternoons on hillside vineyards was ready to be set free and to scatter the fogs of London. Little by little the lawyer's reserve melted. There was no man from whom he kept fewer secrets than Mr. Guest, and he wasn't always sure he kept as many as he meant to. Guest had often been sent on business to the doctor's house; he knew Poole; he could hardly have failed to hear of Mr. Hyde's familiarity about the place; he might draw his own conclusions—so wasn't it just as well, then, that he should see a letter that cleared up that mystery? And all the more since Guest, being a great student and critic of handwriting, would think the step natural and obliging. The clerk, besides, was a man of sound judgment; he could hardly read so strange a document without dropping some remark, and by that remark Mr. Utterson might shape his next move.
“This is a sad business about Sir Danvers,” he said.
“Yes, sir, indeed. It's stirred up a great deal of public feeling,” Guest replied. “The man, of course, was mad.”

“I'd like to hear your thoughts on that,” Utterson replied. “I have a document here in his handwriting; it's strictly between us, since I hardly know what to do about it; it's an ugly business at best. But there it is—right up your alley: a murderer's autograph.”
Guest's eyes lit up, and he sat down at once and studied it eagerly. “No, sir,” he said, “not mad; but it's an odd hand.”
“And by all accounts a very odd writer,” the lawyer added.
Just then the servant came in with a note.
“Is that from Dr. Jekyll, sir?” the clerk asked. “I thought I knew the writing. Anything private, Mr. Utterson?”
“Just an invitation to dinner. Why? Do you want to see it?”

“One moment. I thank you, sir”; and the clerk laid the two sheets of paper side by side and carefully compared their contents. “Thank you, sir,” he said at last, handing both back. “It's a very interesting autograph.”
There was a pause, during which Mr. Utterson struggled with himself. “Why did you compare them, Guest?” he asked suddenly.
“Well, sir,” the clerk replied, “there's a rather striking resemblance; the two hands are identical in many points—only slanted differently.”
“Rather odd,” said Utterson.
“It is, as you say, rather odd,” Guest replied.
“I wouldn't mention this note, you know,” said Utterson.
“No, sir,” said the clerk. “I understand.”

But no sooner was Mr. Utterson alone that night than he locked the note away in his safe, where it stayed from that time forward. “What!” he thought. “Henry Jekyll forge a letter for a murderer!” And his blood ran cold in his veins.
